Welcome. Tonight's hour is content, not logistics: the orientation deck and WTClass carry the mechanics of the semester. What I want you to leave with tonight are four maps and one posture. The four maps: the seven-layer stack, the five-stage progression to agentic AI, the definition of an agent from PEAS to the nine components, and the framework board with every box assigned to a week. The posture: the human is index zero, and here is what happens when the human stops being index zero. Four words describe the semester — survey, build, govern, defend — and tonight is the survey and govern half of that. [0:00–0:02]

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development · Thu 08/27/2026 · 4:00–5:00 · CC209 / Dr. Jeffry Babb · Paul and Virginia Engler College of Business · West Texas A&M University

Five moves. Framing for ten minutes; the two maps for fifteen; what an agent is for thirteen, including the one worked example we do on a slide tonight, a chat assistant against Claude Code; governance for fourteen; and the last eight minutes on the instrument you will use every week and what is due Wednesday. Nothing is on a screen tonight except these slides; the install clinic is in lab at six.

Cut from slide 2 (full wording):
- Layers of AI (and the one everybody forgets); AI & ML → Agentic AI; the framework board, every box assigned to a week
- Russell & Norvig and PEAS; the LLM agent loop and its halt; the nine components; a worked Design Analysis: chat assistant vs. Claude Code

Two questions, one course. The survey question is a why question: not what is fashionable this month, but what problem each design answered and what it cost. The build question is whether you can make one and answer for it. Tree Hollow is your first reading because it names the stake: a system can produce an answer without being able to answer for it. Ask them: who answered for the last piece of generated code you shipped? Sit in the silence for a moment. Then the definition that runs the semester: a language model is a reasoner with no persistent state, no ground truth, and no accountability. Every component we study is an attempt to supply one of those three things from outside the model. Governance supplies the third, and it cannot be automated. [~7 min]

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- Why was each system built that way, what problem did it answer, and what did it cost? Historical order, one component model.
- Answerability / A model has no persistent state, no ground truth, and no accountability. Everything stacked on top of it — tools, memory, evaluators, governance — exists to supply those. The engineer's irreducible role is to be the one who answers. The whole structure of this course (flight cards, consultations, attestations) exists to make that true rather than aspirational.

The first map. Seven layers, read top down or bottom up. Agentic AI on top: memory, planning, tool use, autonomous execution. Underneath it, generative AI, deep learning, neural networks, machine learning, classical AI, and at the bottom the data foundation: ownership, definitions, quality, lineage. The point of drawing it as a widening stack is that every agentic system stands on all of it. Nothing at the top replaces anything below; classical planning did not die, it came back as 'planning' in LLM agents. When you write a Design Analysis you start at the bottom. What does this stand on? [~5 min]

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- How to read it / Agentic AI is thin and new; the foundation is old and cracked. / Every Design Analysis starts at the bottom: what model, what weights, what data does this thing stand on — local or hosted? / Two passes on any system: what does it claim (top-down) and what does it stand on (bottom-up). / The foundation shows through in E7 (memory on embeddings) and E11 (what your evaluation data actually is).

Why is it forgotten? Because it is unglamorous and because it is where the cost lands, later, on someone else. Four words from the framework image: ownership, definitions, quality, lineage. Each one becomes a failure later in the semester. Ownership: who may the agent act on behalf of. Definitions: the agent inherits every ambiguity in your schema, and 'done' is the most dangerous word in the course. Quality: retrieval returns what is stored; in week seven you will poison your own memory with one false fact and watch it propagate. Lineage: without provenance a polished summary becomes a fact; that is the ten-deep summary-laundering chain we read in week nine. The Sprint and Drift essay 'Newtonian motion' makes the general claim: the cost of generated code is deferred, never erased. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- The Newtonian-motion argument: the cost of generated code is deferred, never erased. The foundation is where the bill is delivered.

The second map, five stages left to right. What changes at each step is the unit of work. AI and ML turns data into a decision. Deep learning stacks networks for harder decisions. Generative AI produces an artifact: text, code, an image. AI agents take on a task: they call tools, plan, remember, and keep a human in the loop. Agentic AI automates a process: many agents, protocols between them, delegation, intent preserved across handoffs, rollback, evaluators, cost management, observability, governance. Read the small text in the last two columns; it is the syllabus. The course lives there. Weeks one through seven build the AI Agents column on your system; eight through twelve build the Agentic AI column. [~4 min]

- multi-agent collaboration · agent protocols · delegation & handoff · intent preservation · rollback · feedback loops & evaluators · cost & resource mgmt · observability · governance & guardrails
- The course lives in the last two stages. E1–E7 build the AI Agents column on your system; E8–E12 build the Agentic AI column. Note what changes at each step: the unit of work goes from a decision, to an artifact, to a task, to a process.

The same five stages as a road. Stops one through three are behind us in the sense that you consume them: the models, the networks, the generative capability come from a vendor or an open-weight release. Stops four and five are the ones you build in this course: an agent that takes on a task, then an agentic system that automates a process. Keep this picture; every week I will tell you which stop we are at. [~1 min]

The same board read the other way: as rings out from the foundation. Foundation, creation, core systems, action, full automation. Rings tell you how far a system's capability extends outward; the columns on the previous slide tell you when each capability arrived historically. Hold both readings. The most common thing sold as agentic today claims ring five and runs on ring two: a generative model with a loop bolted on, no memory, no evaluator, no governance. By the end of tonight you will be able to say why that matters. And here is the exercise for the week: mark every box on the board you can already name a concrete system for. The blanks are your reading list. [~3 min]

This is the fill-in order. I have put every box on the framework board somewhere in these twelve weeks. Two things to notice. First, the middle is inverted from the catalog: tools and MCP come before context and memory, because since 2024 most of what fills a context window is tool results, and MCP is a tool protocol that needs function calling understood first. Second, the two starred weeks run on a local open-weight model no matter which route you chose, because tool calling with a small model is instructive precisely because it is brittle, and embeddings are cheap locally. You do not need to memorize this; you need to know it exists so that every week you can say where you are on the board. [~3 min]

Before we define an agent, be precise about the reasoner in the middle of it. What a language model adds is a reasoner that generalizes from text; that is the thing classical agents never had, and it is why 2023 happened. What it does not have is three things: persistent state, ground truth, and accountability. Look at the semester through that lens and it simplifies. Context and memory supply state. Tools, retrieval, and evaluators supply ground truth. Governance supplies accountability, and that is the one that cannot be supplied by more software, because accountability is a property of a person. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- A reasoner that generalizes from text. /  / It can read an unfamiliar error, propose a plan, write the call, and explain itself in prose — the capability that made 2023's explosion possible and that the classical agents of chapter 4 never had.
- It cannot answer for anything. Governance and the human interface (E0, E5, E9, E11) exist to supply it — and this one cannot be automated.

Before the LLM there was a perfectly good definition of an agent and it still holds. Russell and Norvig: an agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators; the agent function maps percept sequences to actions. You specify one by PEAS: performance measure, environment, actuators, sensors. Notice the P. The performance measure is the thing the 2023 loops never wrote down, and it is why they ran until the credit card was empty. The five agent types are a ladder: reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based, learning. And BDI and FIPA are where multi-agent vocabulary comes from; when we meet CrewAI in week eight you will recognize a 1990s design with a language model in the reasoner slot. Your first exercise this week: specify your intended system by PEAS. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- Agent types, in increasing sophistication: simple reflex · model-based · goal-based · utility-based · learning. BDI (belief–desire–intention) and FIPA multi-agent platforms are the pre-LLM coordination vocabulary; we meet them again in E8.

Now put a language model in the reasoner slot. Perceive: the prompt, tool results, files, events. Reason: one model call that emits a thought and a decision. Act: either a tool call or a final answer. Then the question the whole loop turns on: halt? If not, the observation goes back in as the next percept. ReAct, from Yao and colleagues in 2022, is the canonical form: thought, action, observation, interleaved. It is the atom that every later week decorates with tools, memory, coordination, and evaluation. What did it lack? Memory, a budget, verification. And the halt condition is what 2023 forgot: AutoGPT and BabyAGI were this loop with a goal and nothing to stop it. Your first sortie next week is a loop that halts, on every input class, within budget, with every turn in the ledger. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 12 (full wording):
- Thought → Action → Observation, interleaved, until the model emits a final answer. It is the atom every later week decorates. What it lacked: memory, a budget, and verification.
- AutoGPT and BabyAGI (spring 2023) were the loop with goals and no grounding, no budget, no evaluator. They spiraled. A loop without a halt is not autonomy; it is a bill. Sortie 1 is 'a governed loop that halts.'

Nine components. This is how you take every system apart this semester, and the order matters: it goes from what it stands on, to what it sees, to how it thinks, to how it acts, to what it remembers, to how it coordinates, to what checks it, to where the human is, to how it runs. For each one there is a question and, in teal, the failure that shows up when the component is missing or weak. Read the failures as a preview of the incident casebook: injection is a perception failure; a spiral is a planning failure; summary laundering is a coordination failure; governance theater is component eight. A Design Analysis is nine short answers and one paragraph on why. [~3 min]

Here is the exercise for the week, done on a slide. Left column, a chat assistant; right column, an agent harness like Claude Code or Codex CLI. Walk the nine rows. The foundation is the same hosted model. Perception changes: the harness sees the repo, the shell, tool results, an instruction file. Planning changes: the chat has one turn and the human is the loop; the harness runs an open ReAct loop with plan mode and subagents. Tools: none versus a built-in set plus MCP with permission prompts and hooks. Memory: both are window-bound, but the harness compacts and reads an instruction file. Coordination: single versus main session plus subagents. Evaluation: in both, mostly the human. Governance: the chat has a human on every turn by construction; the harness has a human in the loop per tool call, and attestation is implicit. Runtime: a web page versus a terminal with background and cloud sessions. Now the paragraph that matters. The harness owns the loop so the vendor can ship tools, hooks, compaction, and subagents as features; that is what makes it an agent. The cost is that governance is per call and implicit, and nothing records what was attested. That is the gap the reference design fills one tier up. And note: the chat assistant is not worse. It is a workflow with the human as the loop, and most production agents should be workflows. [~4 min]

Cut from slide 14 (full wording):
- The harness owns the loop so the vendor can ship tools, permissions, hooks, compaction, and subagents as product features: that is what turns a generative system into an agent (components 3, 4, 6, 9 appear). /  / The cost: governance is per-call and implicit. Every tool call asks 'allow?', and by week four you are pressing yes without reading. Nothing records what was attested. That gap — component 8 — is what the reference design, gzkit, fills one tier up. /  / The chat assistant is not worse; it is a workflow with the human as the loop. Most production 'agents' should be workflows.

Two distinctions. First, from Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents': a workflow calls the model along code paths you wrote; an agent lets the model direct its own control flow. Most production agents are workflows and should be. You will reach for the open loop only when the path cannot be known ahead of time, and in week two you will have to write down which one you chose and why. Second, the historical point. The pre-LLM era carried forward PEAS, planning, and coordination protocols. What 2023 dropped and the field has been rediscovering ever since: explicit state, halt conditions, and evaluation against an environment. Reinforcement learning already knew about reward hacking; gaming the gate is not new. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 15 (full wording):
- Workflow: the model is called along predefined code paths; control lives in your code. /  / Agent: the model directs its own control flow — decides which tool, when, and whether to continue. /  / Most production 'agents' are workflows, and should be: predictable, cheap, testable. Reach for an open loop only when the path cannot be known in advance. E2 refactors your loop into a named pattern (chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator–workers, evaluator–optimizer) and makes you write down why.
- Carried forward / PEAS and the agent function / Planning (STRIPS → goal decomposition) / Coordination protocols (FIPA, contract net → A2A, crews) / Dropped in 2023, rediscovered since / Explicit state (→ context engineering, ledgers) / Halt conditions and budgets (→ governed loops) / Evaluation against an environment (→ evals as gates); reward hacking (→ gaming the gate, failure mode 9)

Here is why the course is built the way it is, and it comes from gzkit's why.md. Week one you prompt carefully and read every line. Week two you skim the diff and trust the green checkmarks. Week three you batch approvals and 'looks good' becomes reflexive. Week four you are approving pull requests you did not read for code you do not understand. Nobody decides to lose control. It slips away one looks-good at a time. There are three names for it and they are the same failure: cognitive surrender, where the judgment is delegated rather than the task; mediated observation, where you see the summary and never the artifact; and governance theater, where every check passes and nobody verified anything. Ask the room: where on this curve were you last week? The first exercise in chapter three is a one-week log of your own review behavior. [~4 min]

The answer to the Degradation Pattern is the Zero Doctrine: the human is index zero. First in priority: your intent drives every decision. Final in authority: you sign off, not the model. And it cannot be automated away, because accountability is a property of a person. The word zero has its own history in the reference design: it began as zero overhead, became zero drift, and settled as index zero. The covenant is five clauses and both parties are bound. The human defines intent. The agent operates within constraints and flags violations. Verification is mutual. The human attests after observing the artifacts, not the summary. Artifacts survive sessions. The part people miss is that it has two sides: gates constrain the agent, and the human must engage. If you only have gates you get theater. The three concerns, specification, methodology, governance, need each other; the sentence on the slide is the founding argument of the reference design, from a conversation in January in which the model said only specification matters and the operator refused. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 17 (full wording):
- Two sides: gates constrain agents, and humans must engage — read everything, insist on Q&A. Gates alone produce theater. “Specification without governance drifts; governance without methodology is theater; methodology without specification is arbitrary.”

The covenant is enforced by five gates. ADR: intent before implementation. TDD: tests from the spec, and the red witnessed before the green. Docs: what is written matches what runs. BDD: acceptance scenarios for anything with an external contract. Human: someone looked at the artifacts and signed. Two lanes: Lite is gates one and two and that is where your weekly Evolutions live; Heavy is all five and that is the Final System. Ceremony must earn its place, which is why there are two lanes and not one. But human attestation at the brief level is universal, and there is no self-close path. The command doctrine is where the flight vocabulary of this course comes from. Degani and Wiener's Four P's: philosophy, policies, procedures, practices. The cockpit is the model because it is the one place where authority over an automated system has been engineered for decades. Four rules: accountability is non-transferable; authority must be instrumented, not asserted; the model is a crew resource, not a crew member; evidence is artifacts, not narration. [~3 min]

Cut from slide 18 (full wording):
- Degani & Wiener: philosophy → policies → procedures → practices. A cockpit is the model because it is the one place where authority over an automated system has been engineered for decades. /  / • Accountability is non-transferable. / • Authority must be instrumented, not asserted. / • The model is a crew resource, not a crew member. / • Evidence is artifacts, not narration.
- Evolutions run Lite (gates 1–2). The Final System closes out Heavy (1–5). * Brief-level human attestation is universal; there is no self-close path. Closed vocabulary: Completed · Completed — Partial · Dropped.

Situate the posture so nobody mistakes it for the whole of AI governance. Policy frameworks, NIST's risk management framework, the EU AI Act, ISO 42001, tell an organization what must be true; they are silent on what one engineer and one agent do in one session. Frontier-lab safety frameworks and system cards govern the model, and in week eleven you will read one as a Design Analysis. The practitioner literature on auditing names an accountability gap: audits without access, attestations nobody observed. A covenant is one engineer's answer to that gap: below policy, inside the session, at the level of the artifact. It cannot make a model safe or certify an organization. It makes one build answerable. [~2 min]

Cut from slide 19 (full wording):
- Organizational risk management: map, measure, manage, govern. Necessary, and silent on what one engineer and one agent do in one session.
- The industry's evaluation genre: what was tested, what was found. E11 reads one as a Design Analysis. They govern the model, not your use of it.
- Audits without access, standards without enforcement, attestations nobody observed. The practitioner literature names the gap; a covenant is one engineer's answer to it.
- Where it fits: below policy, inside the session, at the level of the artifact. Where it does not: it cannot make a model safe, certify an organization, or substitute for law. It makes one build answerable.

That last one is the whole course in one question. The format is on the right and it is short on purpose: about a hundred and fifty words, nine lines, one paragraph, five items. CIDM6333_E10_Lecture_EvalsAsGates.pptx:
Evolution 10. Last week an adversary from another model family refuted a planted falsehood, and the receipt went in the log. Tonight we turn that move on our own checks. The framing sentence: evaluation is falsification. A check that has never failed tells you nothing about the code it covers. Survey: the agent benchmarks the field has used since 2023, read for what their graders actually check, and what happened to several of them in 2026. Build: a golden set, a regression delta, and a RED witness, wired to a gate that exits non-zero. The lab at six is self-guided and small; the full test points fly in the Sprint, due Wednesday 11/11.

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- Evolution 10 · Lecture · Thu 11/05
- Golden sets, regression deltas, judges and their biases, the RED witness, and pre-registration; what SWE-bench, GAIA, WebArena, AgentBench, and τ-bench measure, and what they hide
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development · 4:00–6:00 · CC209 / Survey: SWE-bench (and Verified, Pro), GAIA, WebArena, AgentBench, τ-bench and τ²-bench; LLM-as-judge; the 2026 benchmark breaks · Build: a golden set, a regression delta, and a RED witness wired to a gate (lab 6:00–6:30, self-guided)

Eight minutes of framing, forty of spine, five on the common mistake, a five-minute break at 0:55, thirty minutes of teardowns, fifteen on the reference design, then the lens, the card, and the lab and Sprint brief. The spine is long tonight because each of its parts is a thing you will build this week: a golden set, a delta, a gate, a judge check, a RED witness, and a pre-registered card. There is no in-class Go/No-Go; your Chase signs the card in the repository before you fly.

Cut from slide 2 (full wording):
- The benchmarks and their graders; SWE-bench Verified retired; the 2026 breaks; MT-Bench as a judge system; Design Analysis of τ²-bench; gzkit eval runner
- Lab 6:00–6:30 (self-guided); Sprint due Wed 11/11; async Go/No-Go and Chase

Framing. Most of you have tests, and most of those tests have only ever been green. A green test that has never been red is a claim about the test. Two rules. First, a check counts only after you have seen it fail with the behavior removed; that is the RED witness, and gzkit's glossary defines it as proof that a test fails without the change it covers. Second, you write down what would count as failure before you look at any result; that is pre-registration, and it is what your flight cards have been since E1. Tonight's claim is the chapter's Sortie 10 claim. Its three falsifiers are the three ways an evaluation suite lies, and the fourth line is the rule the reference design learned: passing by moving the goalposts is a fail.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- Rule one: a check counts only after it has been seen red. Remove the behavior it covers, run it, watch it fail, restore. That is the RED witness. / Rule two: the falsifier is written before the evidence exists. Threshold, cases, and the removal diff are committed before the first run. That is pre-registration.
- Your evaluation suite fails when it should: removing the feature, or planting a wrong answer, turns the gate red. / Three observations falsify it: a green gate with the feature removed; a judge that scores a planted error as correct; a golden case that cannot fail. A pass obtained by editing the golden set or the threshold after the first run is a FAIL, not a pass.

Six words. Task, trial, grader, transcript, and outcome are Anthropic's vocabulary from its January 2026 engineering post on agent evals; I use them because they separate things people blur. A task is the case; a trial is one attempt; the grader scores it; the transcript is how the agent got there; the outcome is the state it left behind. Their advice is to grade the outcome, not the path, because agents find valid routes you did not anticipate. The sixth word is ours: a gate is a grader whose result stops something. An eval that prints a percentage and lets the commit through is a report, and reports get ignored at eleven at night.

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- One input with a stated success criterion. In a golden set, one line of JSONL with an id, the input, the check, and the expected value.
- One attempt at one task. Model outputs vary between trials, so a task with a model in the loop is run more than once.
- The logic that scores a trial: code (equals, contains, schema, a test), a model with a rubric, or a human. One task can carry several graders.
- The full record of a trial: messages, tool calls, intermediate results. Read transcripts; a score without them hides how the agent got there.
- The state of the environment after the trial: the row in the database, the file on disk. Grade the outcome where you can, not the path.
- Our addition. The grader's result wired to a command that exits non-zero and stops the build, the commit, or the release. An eval that only prints a number is a report.
- Vocabulary from Anthropic, 'Demystifying evals for AI agents' (Jan 9, 2026). Code graders are fast, cheap, and reproducible; model graders are flexible and biased; humans calibrate both.

A golden set is a small set of cases you trust enough to stop the build on. The left panel is the format I recommend: one JSON object per line, an id, the requirement it covers, the input, the check, and the expected value. Three check types: equals for anything with one right answer, refused for the must-say-no cases, and judge for open answers, with the rubric in a file. The rules on the right: draw cases from your failures in AI_LOG, not from your successes; tie each to a requirement; make a third of them negatives; keep it small enough that you read every failure; freeze it; and prefer code checks. The judge line is last on purpose.

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- Source. Cases come from AI_LOG and flight-log failures, not from what the system already does well. / Coverage. Every case names the requirement it covers. A requirement with no case is untested; a case with no requirement is noise. / Negatives. At least a third are must-refuse or must-halt cases. An agent that says yes to everything passes a set of positives. / Size. 10–30 cases for a course system. Enough to cover each requirement twice; small enough to read every failure. / Frozen. Changing a case after a run needs a ledger event and a reason. A case edited to pass is metagaming (App. C #9). / Deterministic first. Use code checks wherever the answer is checkable; send only the rest to a judge.

One run is an anecdote. τ-bench, from Yao, Shinn, Razavi, and Narasimhan in June 2024, introduced pass^k: the probability that all k trials of a task succeed. GPT-4o succeeded on fewer than half the tasks, and in the retail domain fewer than a quarter of tasks passed eight trials out of eight. pass@k is the optimist's number and pass^k is the operator's. The second paragraph is the distinction Anthropic draws: capability suites are meant to start low and climb; regression suites sit near a hundred and any drop is a bug. Your gate is a regression suite. The practical rule: any case with a model in it runs three times, and you report pass^3.

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- pass@k is the chance that at least one of k trials succeeds. It rises with k, so it flatters. pass^k is the chance that all k succeed. It falls with k, and it is the number a user who runs the task every day experiences. / Two kinds of suite. A capability suite asks what the agent can do; it starts low and is meant to climb. A regression suite asks whether it still does what it did; it sits near 100%, and any drop is a defect. Your Sortie 10 gate is a regression suite with a few capability cases reported beside it. / For your card: run every model-in-the-loop case at least 3 times and report pass^3 alongside the mean.

The gate in five steps. Run and write per-case results. Compare against a baseline you froze and committed. Decide with a rule written in code before you ran it: any regression, or a rate below the threshold, exits one. Name the cases, because a red light with no case id sends you hunting. Wire it into something that runs without you: a hook or CI. The strip is the reason for case-by-case comparison. An aggregate of eighty percent last week and eighty percent this week can hide one requirement that broke and another that improved. gzkit's runner has a function named eval_regression_delta for the same reason; we will see it in the reference design.

Four biases, each with a paper you can cite in your Design Analysis. Position: Wang and colleagues showed in 2023 that reordering two answers was enough for a weaker model to beat a stronger one on sixty-six of eighty queries. Verbosity: the MT-Bench paper, Zheng and colleagues at NeurIPS 2023, found judges prefer longer answers. Self-preference: Zheng named it self-enhancement; Panickssery, Bowman, and Feng in 2024 showed models recognize their own outputs and that recognition predicts the preference; Wataoka and colleagues argue the mechanism is familiarity, lower perplexity. Injection is the 2026 addition: the Berkeley group put hidden comments in agent answers and moved the judge's score. The right column is what you build: both orders, binary rubric, a different family, and the answer treated as data, which is the E5 rule again.

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- Wang et al. (2023), 'Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators': by swapping answer order alone, Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries as judged by an LLM.
- Judge every pair in both orders. Count a verdict only if both orders agree; a flip is a tie and goes to a human.
- Zheng et al. (2023) name self-enhancement. Panickssery, Bowman & Feng (2024): models recognize their own text, and self-recognition tracks self-preference. Wataoka et al. (2024): judges favor low-perplexity, familiar text.
- The judge is a different model family from the generator. Strip model names and signatures from what the judge sees.
- Wang, Mang, Cheung, Sen & Song (UC Berkeley, Apr 2026): hidden comments in an agent's answer steered an LLM judge's score (CAR-bench).
- Zheng et al. also found GPT-4 judges agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time, the same rate humans agree with each other. Agreement is the reason judges are used; the biases are the reason they are checked.

The RED witness, in one sentence from gzkit's own glossary: proof that a test fails without the change it covers. The procedure is on the slide: rebuild without the change, run the covering test, expect failure, restore. The idea is old. TDD makes you watch the test fail first; mutation testing, from DeMillo, Lipton, and Sayward in 1978, changes the program on purpose and asks whether the suite notices. For an eval suite you want two witnesses: remove the feature, and plant a wrong answer. The third paragraph names what they catch: tautological tests, where the expected value came from the code under test, and hollow tests, which pass for any output. You will find one of each in the lab tonight. Verify the gz arb red flags before class.

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- Where the idea comes from. Test-driven development writes the test first and watches it fail (red) before the code makes it pass (green). Mutation testing (DeMillo, Lipton & Sayward, 1978) generalizes it: change the program on purpose; a suite that still passes has not tested what changed. gzkit calls the recorded version a RED witness and runs it with gz arb red. [Verify the command's current flags against the repository before class.] / For an eval suite, two witnesses. (1) Feature removed: comment out the behavior; the cases that cover it must go red, and you predicted which ones before you ran it. (2) Wrong answer planted: substitute one wrong output; the grader or judge must fail it. / What it catches. A tautological test compares the code with itself (expected value computed by the function under test). A hollow test passes for any output (assert result is not None; a check that accepts every label). Both are green forever, and both look like coverage.

Pre-registration is the flight card's origin outside aviation. Nosek and colleagues in PNAS in 2018 put it as prediction versus postdiction: a hypothesis fixed before the data tests something; one fitted after only describes it. Kerr's 1998 paper named the failure HARKing. In an eval suite, HARKing looks like choosing the threshold after the score, dropping the failing case, re-running until green, or padding the set with cases you already pass. Our mechanism: commit the card and the golden set first, put the hash on the card, and have the Chase sign that commit. The strip is the test you apply to every card this week.

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- State the hypothesis, the measure, and the decision rule before observing the outcome. Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven & Mellor (PNAS, 2018): pre-registration separates prediction, which tests a claim, from postdiction, which only generates one.
- HARKing, hypothesizing after the results are known (Kerr, 1998). In evals: choosing the threshold after seeing the score; dropping the case that failed; re-running until green; adding a case the system already passes.
- The card holds the claim, the threshold, the case count, the removal diff, and the falsifiers. Commit it and the golden set before the first run; the commit hash goes on the card. The Chase signs that commit. Amendments append with a reason; they never overwrite.
- The test for pre-registration: could the evidence have come out against you, and did you say in advance what that would look like?

The common mistake of the week. Recording the agent's current output as the expected value is quick, and it produces a set that is green on day one and blind to any bug present on that day. It detects change, which has some value, but it never checked correctness. Its cousins are the not-None assertion, the judge asked whether an answer is good with no reference, and a fixture that mocks the thing under test. On the board: remove the feature and some snapshot cases do go red; then plant a bug that was present on snapshot day, and nothing goes red. The rule: expected values come from requirements, written by hand before the agent runs.

Cut from slide 12 (full wording):
- Common mistake: goldens copied from the system's own output
- for case in inputs: /     case['expect'] = agent(case['input'])  # 'record the golden' / json.dump(cases, open('golden.json', 'w')) / The set now encodes whatever the agent did on the day you ran it, bugs included. Every case passes on the first run. It will catch a change, but not a wrong behavior that was already there, and it never asked whether the output was right. / Cousins: assert result is not None; a judge asked 'is this a good answer?'; a fixture that mocks the feature under test.
- 1. Take the snapshot set. Remove the feature. Some cases go red: good. / 2. Now plant a bug that was present on snapshot day (the agent always called a write tool 'write', even for delete). Nothing goes red, because the golden says 'write'. / 3. Fix: write expected values from the requirement, by hand, before running the agent. Snapshots are allowed only as a change detector, labeled as such, beside the golden set. / Rule for Sortie 10: every expected value in golden.jsonl traces to a requirement or an AI_LOG entry, never to a run.

The judge as a system. MT-Bench is eighty multi-turn questions graded by GPT-4; Chatbot Arena is crowdsourced pairwise votes between anonymous models. The design choice is to replace human raters with a model, justified by agreement above eighty percent, which matched human-to-human agreement. The cost is that the judge's biases are in every score, and the paper measured them: position, verbosity, self-enhancement. The failure mode is metagaming at scale: optimize against a judge and you learn the judge. The strip is the habit I want in your Design Analysis: when you cite this paper for the eighty percent, cite it for the biases too.

Cut from slide 17 (full wording):
- Teardown: MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, the judge as a system
- 80 multi-turn questions (MT-Bench) graded by GPT-4 as judge, in single-answer and pairwise modes; Chatbot Arena collects crowd votes between two anonymous models. 3K expert votes and 30K conversations released.
- Replace human raters with a strong model, because humans are slow and costly. Justified by agreement: GPT-4 matched human preference over 80% of the time, the same as human-human agreement.
- The judge's biases enter every score: position, verbosity, self-enhancement, limited reasoning on math. The paper measured them and proposed swaps and reference answers; users of the method often skip both.
- App. C #9 at scale: a system tuned against a judge learns the judge. Longer, more confident answers score higher whether or not they are right. Defense: the admissibility checks from 0:38.

The live Design Analysis. We fill it on the board together, and this slide is the answer key. The interesting rows are three. Tools: in the telecom domain the user also has tools, which is what dual control means, so the agent must get a person to do things, not just do them itself. Evaluation: the grader compares the final database with the goal state, which is outcome grading, and pass^k measures consistency. Governance: the human is simulated by a model, so the benchmark has a model inside its own grading path, and any simulator error lands on the agent's score. The judgment loop is in the strip; write your own before you look at mine.

- Agent tools on the backend; in telecom, the user also has tools on their own device (dual control, modeled as a Dec-POMDP).
- Agent and user must coordinate: the agent guides a user who acts. Ablations separate reasoning errors from communication errors.
- Final database state compared with the goal state; pass^k over repeated trials. Graded by outcome, not transcript.
- The human is simulated, and the simulator is a model: its errors become the agent's score.

Weak: goldens copied from the system, single runs, a gate that only prints, a judge grading its own family in one order, goalposts moved after the run, and a removal claim with no prediction. Sound: a small tied set with negatives, a committed baseline and a named delta, a pre-registered commit, a removal that turns exactly the predicted cases red, pass^3 for model cases, and an admissible judge. Exceptional: the stub finds and fixes a hollow case, the judge is calibrated and survives an injection, the gate refuses a real push, and you have checked that your agent cannot reach the answers, which is the Berkeley lesson applied at home.

The book's thesis sentence is the quote: a system can produce an answer without being able to answer for it. Tonight that becomes two rules. First, the black box outranks the narrative: the model's account of what it did is a claim, your summary is a claim, and only a trace or a receipt is evidence. Second, a guardrail is a mechanism at a place where it can refuse, like a permission deny, a server-side check, or a commit-time check, and it earns credit only when an attack reached it and the trace shows the refusal. The claim is the chapter's Sortie 11 claim, and the third falsifier is the one students miss: an attack the system never received proves nothing about the guardrail.

Four records, four questions. A trace is a tree of spans for one run: the agent invocation at the top, model calls and tool calls under it, each timed and carrying attributes. A receipt is narrower and stricter: it records the observed result of a command, the exit status, the duration, the git state, and the tail of stdout, and it validates against a schema. The ledger is the project's runtime truth, the append-only log of decisions and attestations. The transcript is what the model said, and this is where students get caught: the model's sentence 'I did not read the env file' is a claim, and the tool span is the evidence. Tonight's lab makes you check one against the other.

This is the mistake I expect in a third of the logs. 'All five attacks failed' written from the model's final message and a clean file. The black box tells a different story: two payloads never entered the loop, and a third was refused by the model before any tool call, so the guardrail the card named was never exercised. Model refusal is a real outcome and you record it, but it is a property of this model on this day, and the next model may comply. The guardrail is what stands when the model does not refuse. So each attack needs two pieces of evidence: the delivery span and the refusal span.

Disclosed by Aonan Guan with colleagues from Johns Hopkins in April. One pattern, three agents. Claude Code's security reviewer took the pull-request title into its prompt and ran a process listing that exposed its keys, which went into a PR comment. Gemini's action followed a fake trusted section in an issue comment. Copilot's agent read an HTML comment nobody sees in the rendered issue, base64-encoded the process listing so secret scanning would not match, and committed it through the one channel it was allowed to use. Read for mechanism: in all three, untrusted text reached a loop that held secrets and a write path. His point about blocklists is the lab's point: deny ps and the attacker reads /proc instead. Note also, per VentureBeat's reading, that Anthropic's Opus 4.7 card had said the security-review action was not hardened against injection; the system card was a threat model the integrators did not read.

- Aonan Guan's root cause: the agent holds production secrets because it needs them, and processes untrusted input because that is its job. His defense: allowlists of tools and secrets, not blocklists.

Three stacks, read for the design choice. Langfuse is open source, built on OpenTelemetry, and has a guardrail observation type, which tells you its designers expected guardrails to be traced. It joined ClickHouse in January and says the licence is not changing. LangSmith is proprietary, accepts OTLP, and groups traces into threads by a metadata key that every child run must carry, or the cost roll-up is wrong. OpenCode has no tracing product, but its session export already holds the facts: tool, status, times, tokens, cost. Failure modes: every stack will happily store a secret you let into the content, and OpenCode's share command publishes a session to a public URL. The lab uses the export, and sets share to disabled.

Evolution 12, the last lecture. For eleven weeks your system has worked on your laptop while you watched it. Tonight it becomes something that runs when you are not watching, and that you can take back when it goes wrong. The framing sentence: a system is operated when someone other than its author can release it, see which version is live, and roll it back from a written page. Survey: the background agents that the vendors now run for you in the cloud and on a schedule, read for who attests an unattended run. Build: serve, package, release, and roll back, with the rollback in the ledger. Code freeze is Monday; ceremonies are Tuesday through Thursday next week, and you book them on Calendly tonight.

- Evolution 12 · Lecture · Thu 11/19
- CIDM 6333 · Agentic Systems Design and Development · 4:00–6:00 · CC209 / Survey: background and cloud agents (Codex cloud, Copilot cloud agent, Claude Code cloud sessions, routines, and GitHub Actions) · gzkit closeout, patch release, MX   ·   Build: your system served, packaged, released, and rolled back in one governed command (lab 6:00–6:30) / Code freeze Mon 11/23 · closeout ceremonies Tue–Thu 11/24–26 by appointment

Eight minutes of framing, forty-five of spine in two halves, a five-minute break at 0:55, thirty minutes of teardowns including one Design Analysis on the board, fifteen on the reference design, and the last fifteen on the lens, the card, the ceremony, and the lab. There is no Go/No-Go in the room tonight. Your Chase signs your card in the repository by Friday night, as in the last several weeks.

Framing. Working means it ran for you, on your machine, while you watched. Operated means a second person can release it, tell which version is live, and roll it back from a written page. Two rules. First, a release is a thing: an artifact with a version and a hash, and a rollback reinstalls that thing. If your rollback is check out the old tag and rebuild, you are releasing a new, untested artifact that happens to share a version number, and I will show you the two hashes later. Second, secrets are injected at run time and appear nowhere else, including the model's context. The claim comes from chapter twenty-one, with one addition: the rollback must name the same hash that was released. The last falsifier is the Heavy lane's: a release with no attestation event is not a release.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- The release is a thing, not a moment. A built artifact (a wheel or an image) with a version and a hash. Rollback reinstalls a thing that already exists. It never rebuilds from an old commit. / Secrets are injected at run time. The key reaches the process from the environment. It is never in the image, the log, the repository, or the model's context.
- A release of your system can be rolled back in one governed command; the rollback is in the ledger and names the same artifact hash that was released; and a planted canary secret appears in no image layer, log, or commit. / Falsifiers: a rollback that needs a manual step; a rollback whose hash differs from the release it restores; the canary found in any artifact; a release with no attestation event.

Chapter twenty-one, section one. An agent is served either as a service or as a job, and you choose before you choose a framework. A service has a waiting caller, so it needs a time budget, idempotency, streaming for long answers, and a health route. A job has no waiting caller, so it needs a budget in turns and dollars, an artifact as its output, and an exit code the scheduler can read. Most of your systems are jobs that you will wrap as a service for the demo, and that is fine if the ADR says so. The failure I see every term is the service with job semantics: a long loop behind a POST, a client that times out and retries, and three copies of the agent spending your budget on the same task.

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- A caller sends a request and waits. FastAPI or an equivalent in front of your loop. / Every request has a time budget; the loop halts inside it / A retried POST must not run the agent twice: idempotency key / Long answers stream; the client sees progress / /health reports status and version
- A trigger starts a run; nobody waits on a socket. A CLI entry point, a cron line, a scheduled cloud agent. / The run has a turn and dollar budget, not a request timeout / Output is an artifact: a branch, a report, a ledger entry / Someone reads the result later; the result must say what it did / Exit code is the only status the scheduler sees
- Most course systems are jobs that someone wraps as a service for the demo. Either is fine. Pick one in an ADR and state the lifecycle. / The mistake is a service with job semantics: a POST that starts a ten-minute loop, a client that times out at 60 seconds and retries, and three agents doing the same work with your key.
- A request that outlives its caller becomes an orphan. Decide who owns the halt: the loop's budget or the server's timeout.

Thirty lines, and every one of them is a decision from the last slide. The limit comes from the environment. The API key is read at startup inside the lifespan handler, so a missing key stops the process at boot instead of at the first request; that is Nygard's Fail Fast. Health returns the installed version, which is how you will see a rollback from outside. The run route takes an idempotency key as a header, so a client retry returns the first result instead of starting a second agent, and it wraps the loop in a timeout, so the halt happens inside the caller's budget and the caller gets a 504 that says so. I ran this with the test client this week: a repeated key calls the loop once, a slow task returns 504, a missing key header returns 422. The idempotency store is in memory; name that limit in your runbook.

Five concerns, each with a wrong place, a right place, and a check a peer can run without your help. The row to slow down on is secrets. An ENV line or a COPY of a dot-env file in a Dockerfile puts the key into a layer, and every pull of that image carries it; a later layer that deletes the file does not remove it from history. Inject at run time from an untracked file or a store, and check with a canary: a fake key with a unique string that you plant in your environment, then search the image history, the logs, and the git log for it. Rate limits: the provider's limit is not your limit. Your system needs its own budget per run and per key, and exceeding it on purpose is a test point. The note is FastAPI's own container guidance, checked this week.

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- FastAPI's container guidance: one process per container; use the exec form of CMD so lifespan shutdown runs; add --proxy-headers behind a TLS proxy (fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/docker).
- A secret in any layer of an image is in every copy of that image forever. Deleting it in a later layer does not remove it.

Two ways to ship the same thing, and the lab offers both because laptops differ. On the left, uv's own commands: bump the version, build a wheel into dist, install it into a separate environment that plays production. Rollback is reinstalling the prior wheel, and the wheel's hash is in the release record. On the right, an image. The one point to take away from the right panel: a tag is a pointer, and the next docker build with the same tag moves it. The image ID or the registry digest is the release. Both columns end with the same strip: a version is a name; record the hash when you release and check it when you roll back.

The release record holds the wheel's SHA-256; the rollback checks it before it installs. / Works on every laptop in the room. No daemon, no admin rights.
- docker build -t myagent:0.1.1 .  (or podman build) / The tag is a pointer. The image ID (or the registry digest) is the release. Record the ID in the release event, because a tag can be moved to a different image by the next build. / Rollback: stop the running container and start the prior image by ID or by a tag you have verified still points at that ID. / Needs Docker or Podman. Not every laptop can run it; that is why the lab does not require it.
- A version number is a name. The hash is the release. Record the hash when you release and check it when you roll back.

Section three of the chapter asks who attests an unattended run. The vendors have converged on five controls, and you will see each of them in the teardowns. A stored trigger, which proves somebody wrote the prompt earlier and proves nothing about whether this run's actions were approved. An isolated environment with network limited by default. A narrow write path: one branch with a prefix, no merge. A human merge. And a record that someone reads, because a green status only says the process exited. Anthropic's routines documentation says that last point in so many words. For your system: if you schedule anything, the scheduled run writes to its own branch or its own file and a person accepts it, and the ledger shows both.

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- The prompt and schedule are written ahead of time by an authorized person. The firing is evidence of storage, not of consent for this run's actions.
- One branch with a known prefix (copilot/, claude/, codex/). No push to a protected branch; no merge by the agent.
- A run log exists. A green status means the run exited; it does not mean the task succeeded. Somebody reads the transcript.
- Fresh VM or runner per run; network limited by default; secrets held outside the sandbox where the vendor supports it.
- Nobody watched the run, so the run's record must answer three questions: what did it change, under whose authority, and who accepted it.

Nygard's second edition, 2018, which is on the reading list. Six cards from the stability chapters that map onto an agent loop. Timeouts on every call, and his advice not to retry at once, because a timeout usually means the fault is still there. Circuit Breaker on a flaky provider, with the state visible in health. Steady State, which is the one students forget: every store that grows needs a purge. Fail Fast, which you just saw in the lifespan handler. Then the two that speak most directly to automation. Force Multiplier is the antipattern: automation that spreads one bad decision everywhere, and a scheduled agent is exactly that. Governor is the answer: resistance in the unsafe direction, so that a person can step in. That is the confirmation gate you built in week three, applied to deployment.

Cut from slide 9 (full wording):
- Every model call and tool call has one. Nygard: do not retry at once after a timeout; the fault is probably still there. Queue or halt.
- After N failures from a provider or tool, stop calling it for a period and fail the run with a reason. Expose the breaker's state in /health.
- Check the key, the model route, and the budget before the first turn. A run that cannot finish should not start.
- Slow automation down in the unsafe direction so a human can intervene: deletes, deploys, mass writes need a pause and a person.
- Automation that amplifies one wrong decision across the fleet. A background agent on a schedule is a force multiplier for whatever its prompt gets wrong.
- The Governor is the pattern the course has been building since E3: a write needs a confirmation event, and an irreversible act needs a human.

All term you ran the Lite lane, gates one and two, ADR and tests. The Final System runs the Heavy lane, and the three gates a release adds are here. Docs: the docs describe the release that exists, and the test is to paste every command from the runbook. BDD: scenarios for the contract a caller relies on, and they run. Human: an attestation event in the ledger with one of three words, recorded by you. You have seen the reference design's incidents where an agent recorded an attestation that was never given; that is why the agent never records Gate 5. Last card: the changelog is for maintainers, the release notes are for the person who has to upgrade or roll back.

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- The README, the runbook, and the release notes describe the release that exists. A command in the docs that fails when pasted is a gate failure.
- Scenarios for the external contract: what a caller of /runs, or a user of the CLI, can rely on. Given, when, then; executed, not just written.
- A person attests: Completed, Completed — Partial, or Dropped. The attestation is an event in the ledger. The agent never records it for you.
- The changelog is every change, for maintainers. Release notes are what a user must know to upgrade and to roll back. Both name the version and the date.
- Chapter 21.5: docs gate; BDD for external contracts; human attestation; release notes vs. changelog; the distribution invariant; MX mode. The reference design segment covers the last two.

The common mistake, and I made it on purpose this week while writing the lab. I built version 0.1.0, released it, recorded its hash. Then I set the version back and built again, which is what a rollback by rebuild does. Same file name, same version string, different bytes: the first eight characters of the two hashes are on the slide. The rollback installed the new file, health said 0.1.0, and only the hash showed that the thing running was not the thing I had released. In my run the smoke test caught it because the code had changed; if the change had been subtle, nothing would have. The fix is in the strip, and it is the lab's step four: keep released artifacts out of the build's reach, and make rollback compare hashes.

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- What happened. The version was set back to 0.1.0 and uv build ran again. The new wheel overwrote the old one at the same path. The rollback installed it, and the ledger recorded a rollback to 0.1.0 with a hash that did not match the release it claimed to restore. / Why it passes a careless check. The version string is right, the file name is right, and health reports 0.1.0. Only the hash shows that the thing running is not the thing that was released.
- Keep every released artifact where a build cannot overwrite it, and make the rollback refuse a hash that differs from the release event.

Five systems, one table, read for runtime and governance. Codex cloud runs a container per task, runs your setup script with network, then blocks network in the agent phase by default. Copilot's agent was renamed from coding agent to cloud agent on April first; it runs in an ephemeral Actions environment with a 59-minute cap, behind a firewall, and it can only push to its own branch. Claude Code's cloud sessions run in an isolated VM with a network allowlist by default; routines are the scheduled and triggered form, hourly at most frequent, and they push to claude-prefixed branches as your GitHub identity. The GitHub Action is the agent as a CI job, so it inherits whatever permissions and secrets the workflow has. Across all five, the agent never merges. Verify every cell before class; these pages change monthly.

Copilot's agent, read for the four things we always read for. The mechanism: a task arrives, the agent runs in an Actions environment you can prepare with a setup-steps workflow, and it pushes to one branch and opens a draft. The design choice is to place the human gate in the pull request, where developers already work, and to deny the agent every action that would close that gate itself: no ready-for-review, no approve, no merge, and no CI run until a person approves it. The cost is minutes, credits, and review load. The failure modes are metagaming the gate, a PR that satisfies the checks but not the task, and safeguard circumvention if the agent can edit the workflow that checks it. The strip: the commits carry the assigner as co-author, which records who asked; nothing records who checked except the review.

- Put the human gate where developers already look: the pull request. Only users with write access can start it. It cannot mark its PR ready, approve, or merge. Actions workflows on its PR do not run until a person clicks Approve and run workflows.

- Commits are authored by Copilot with the assigning developer as co-author, and signed. Attribution answers who asked; it does not answer who checked.

Scheduled agents. The routines documentation is unusually direct, and I quote it on the left: the trigger attests only that the prompt was stored ahead of time, it is not consent for the actions of the run, text sent with a fire is wrapped as untrusted, and a green status does not mean the task succeeded. Read that against Appendix C. Hallucinated authorization is acting as if the schedule were the approval. Fabrication by status is reporting green as done. And a nightly schedule is Nygard's force multiplier. The Governor for your system is simple: a scheduled run writes only to its own branch or file, a person accepts it, and the ledger has two events, not one.
