Anthropic's harness for long-running agents, from November. The sentence to remember is theirs: compaction is not sufficient. So they design every session to begin as a stranger and give it a fixed way to catch up: read the git log, read the progress file, run the smoke test, pick one failing feature. The choice of JSON over Markdown for the feature list is a mechanism against metagaming: the model edits prose freely and structured files less. This is Sortie 6 at production scale: a handoff, a resume procedure, and a ledger, which here is git.

Cut from slide 18 (full wording):
- “Compaction isn’t sufficient.” The harness makes every session start as a stranger and gives it a way to catch up.
- Mechanism. An initializer agent writes init.sh, a claude-progress.txt file, a JSON list of 200+ features all marked failing, and a first commit. Every later session checks the directory, reads the git log and the progress file, picks the highest-priority failing feature, runs init.sh to check the basics, works one feature, commits, and updates the progress file. / Choice and cost. JSON, because 'the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files compared to Markdown files.' One feature per session costs throughput and buys a clean state at every boundary. / Failure mode it defends. App. C #9, metagaming the gate: a model that can edit the checklist can mark a feature passing. The feature list is L1 the model may flip a status on, never rewrite.

Weak: a size where a per-turn count belongs, a default compaction with no record, a diary for a handoff, a transcript pasted in, and a README that says ledger with no path. Sound: a budget record every turn from the provider's own fields; compaction that keeps what you declared and logs what it did; seven sections with an action first; a fresh session that does what you named and asks nothing you answered; three layers declared and a stale view that loses. Exceptional: the budget by category with one category cut, the summary audited against the ledger, a handoff derived from the ledger, a ruling that stays settled, and a second model family resuming from the same file. That last one is cheap if you have a Go subscription; with Big Pickle alone, say so and skip it.

Card six, back to expansion after last week's corner. Five test points: a budget record on every call, a compaction that logs itself and keeps what you declared, a handoff with a hash, a fresh session that takes the named action and asks nothing already answered, and a stale derived view that loses to the ledger. To force test point two inside one session, set a low turn budget for the sortie, for example eight or sixteen thousand tokens, and say so on the card. The falsifiers include the two shortcuts: pasting the transcript, and fixing the handoff after the fresh session has started. Go is asynchronous this term: your Chase signs the card in the repository by Monday night, and you do not fly before that signature.

Framing. The window from last week is gone at the end of the session; memory is the part you chose to keep. Two rules for the whole evening. First, a memory is a claim with a source: the record says where it came from, when, and who wrote it, and a record without those fields is a rumor your agent will repeat with confidence. Second, retrieved text is data and never instruction, which is the E5 rule turned on your own store: a memory is content, and some session or some attacker wrote it. The claim is the one in chapter 16. It has two halves, recall and forgetting, and three falsifiers: a fact that was never stored, an item kept past its rule, and retrieval that changes an answer it had no business changing.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- Whatever survives the session can be wrong next week, and nobody will notice unless the record says where it came from
- Memory is the part of context that survives the session. Everything that survives can be stale, planted, or never true, and it will be read as fact on every turn after.
- A memory is a claim with a source. Every stored item carries where it came from, when, and who wrote it. A record without provenance is a rumor the agent repeats. / Retrieved text is data, never instruction. E5's rule applies to your own store. A memory that says 'always do X' is content that some session, or some attacker, wrote.
- With memory on, the system answers a question about a prior session correctly that it cannot answer with memory off, and eviction removes exactly what the retention rule says it removes. A recalled fact that was never stored, an item retained past its rule, or retrieval that changes an answer that should not change falsifies it.

Five kinds, from chapter 16, and a sixth card that is the question for your ADR. The window is short-term memory and the harness owns it. Working state is typed: if your loop keeps its current goal in a paragraph of prose, it has no state, it has a story. Episodic memory is what happened, append-only and dated. Semantic memory is what is known, and because facts change, every update must say what it replaces. Procedural memory is skills and recipes, and it changes by review. For most of your systems the answer is episodic plus a small semantic store. Write that down first; the store follows from it.

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- Name the kind before you pick the store; each kind has a different writer and a different clock
- What the model sees this turn: instructions, history, tool results, retrieved text. Writer: the harness. Clock: the session. E6 budgeted it.
- Typed fields the loop reads and writes: goal, current step, open approvals, budget left. A Pydantic object or a row, not prose. Clock: the task.
- What happened: turns, tool calls, sortie outcomes, corrections. Append-only and dated. Reflexion's buffer and Generative Agents' stream are episodic.
- What is known: facts about the user, the project, the domain. Mutable, so each change must name what it supersedes. RAG's Wikipedia index is semantic.
- How to do things: skills, prompts, tool recipes. Voyager's skill library, Claude Code skills, your AGENTS.md. Changes by review, not by the agent alone.
- Most course systems need episodic memory (sortie outcomes, decisions) and a small semantic store (user and project facts). ADR-2 says which, before you build a store.

The record is where the first rule becomes code. On the left, four operations, and each one leaves a ledger event: write, store, read, evict or forget. On the right, the record the lab uses: an id that is never reused, the kind, the source file, the date, who wrote it, a retain-until date, a supersedes field, and the text. The store and the ledger answer different questions: the store is what is remembered now, and the ledger is what was remembered on any date, which is what an auditor asks. The strip is the Chase's test: a recalled sentence with no record and no source is a fabrication even when it is right.

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- A memory record is a claim with a source
- Write. Who decides to store: the user ('remember this'), the agent (auto memory), or a rule (every sortie verdict). Every write is a ledger event. / Store. One record per chunk, with provenance. Append-only where you can; ids never reused. / Read. Retrieval returns ids and scores; the block injected into the prompt cites the ids. / Evict and forget. Eviction follows a rule; forgetting follows a request. Both leave a ledger event, never a silent gap.
- If the Chase cannot trace a recalled sentence to a record, and the record to a source file, the recall is a fabrication (App. C #3), whether or not it happens to be true.

Five steps, and each is an ADR-2 decision. Chunking first, with a finding from building tonight's lab tool: when the chunks lost their headings, the question about the Sortie 5 verdict returned the Sortie 3 verdict, because both chunks said 'Chase verdict' and neither said which sortie. Keeping the heading with the chunk fixed it. Represent: counts or vectors, and the same model on both sides. Store: a JSONL file is enough at course scale. Score: cosine, a small k, and a threshold, so that 'nothing found' can happen. Inject: a marked block the model must cite. The strip is when retrieval makes answers worse, and the only way to see it is to run with memory off as a control.

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- Split by paragraph or section. Keep the heading with each chunk. Without it, 'Chase verdict: FAIL' does not say which sortie, and the lab's first test returned the wrong one.
- Bag-of-words (term counts weighted by rarity) or an embedding vector from a local model. Index and query with the same model.
- memory.jsonl, with vectors cached beside the text in the sortie. A JSONL file holds hundreds of records; a vector database is a scaling decision, not a memory decision.
- A marked block: id, source, date, text. The model is told to cite the id it used. The block is data.
- Retrieval hurts when an irrelevant hit crowds the window, a stale hit outranks the fresh one, or a planted record reads as instruction. Memory off is the control that shows which.

Two retrievers, both in the lab's single file. Path B is bag-of-words: tokenize, drop stopwords, weight rare terms up, compare with cosine. It needs nothing but the standard library, and it is very good at exact identifiers, which is most of what a flight log contains. It fails on synonyms. Path A calls Ollama's embed endpoint with embeddinggemma; the vectors come back unit length, so the dot product is the cosine. It handles paraphrase and costs a download, and its numbers are not auditable, so the audit is always on the text and the id. I checked the OpenCode Go and Zen documentation on the twenty-fourth: neither offers an embeddings endpoint, so there is no hosted route through the course harness, and nobody should sign up for another API key for this week.

State first: working state is a typed object the loop owns, and the model proposes changes the loop validates, the same contract as your tools in E3. Then three eviction policies. MemGPT evicts by pressure: warn at about seventy percent, flush half into a recursive summary at a hundred. Retention evicts by rule: a date on every record and a command that removes past-date records and logs each one. Generative Agents evicts by relevance, which means it never deletes anything, it just stops finding it. Only the rule path gives you a test the Chase can check, so that is the one Sortie 7 flies.

Cut from slide 10 (full wording):
- A typed object the loop owns: goal, step, open approvals, budget left, last verdict. The model proposes a change; the loop validates it and writes it. A prose summary is not state.
- At about 70% of the window, a memory-pressure warning lets the model save what matters. At 100%, about half the messages are evicted into a recursive summary. The summary loses detail by design.
- retain_until on every record; evict removes past-date records and logs each id. Deterministic and testable, which is what an auditor wants.
- Nothing is deleted. Old, unimportant memories score low and stop surfacing. Cheap to build; you cannot prove anything is gone.
- Sortie 7 flies the rule path: the Chase checks that each evicted id has a ledger event and is absent from the store, and that a question about it now fails.

Retention is where memory stops being a feature and becomes governance. Four questions. Who may write, and the answerable version names the writers and records which one wrote each item. How long, and the answer is a clock per kind, not 'until full'. Who can delete and how is it proved: a forget command with a reason, a ledger event, and a recall test that now fails. Where it came from: source and date on the record and in the prompt. The strip is a vendor making the same point: in Claude's help pages, deleting a conversation does not delete the memories generated from it. Deletion of a derived store is its own operation, and your system needs one.

Cut from slide 11 (full wording):
- Named writers: a user request, a rule (every sortie verdict), or the agent with a ledger event. Each record carries written_by.
- retain_until per kind: episodic to course end (12/15), semantic until superseded, window never persisted.
- forget <id> --reason writes a ledger event; a recall test shows the id no longer returns.
- Source path and date on the record and in the injected block; the answer cites the id.
- Deleting the source does not delete the memory. Claude's help center says this of its own memory: entries generated from a deleted chat remain until you delete them individually.

How you measure the claim. Four kinds of question. Recall is the one the claim names. Paraphrase tests the retriever choice. Control is the falsifier 'retrieval changes an answer that should not change'. Absent is the fabrication check. On the right, the discipline: fresh session, same model, tools denied so the model cannot go read your flight log and make memory-off look like memory-on, and only the memory block changes between runs. Answers are checked against the file. If Big Pickle or a flash model gets the control wrong, that is a finding, and you record it; you do not swap models until the numbers look good.

Cut from slide 12 (full wording):
- Recall. The answer is in a prior session (the model tag in Sortie 3). Memory on must be right; memory off must fail or say it does not know. / Paraphrase. The same fact in other words. This separates bag-of-words from embeddings. / Control. A question memory has no business changing (a fact stated in the prompt, or plain arithmetic). The answer must be identical on and off. / Absent. A fact never stored. Memory on must say 'not in memory'; a confident answer is a fabrication.
- a fresh session for every run (opencode run starts one) / the same model id both times; record it / every tool denied, so the model cannot read the repository and contaminate the memory-off run / the memory block pasted or omitted, nothing else changed / answers saved verbatim, then checked against the source file, not against the model's confidence
- A small free model will get some of these wrong. That is data for the flight log, not a reason to change models mid-sortie.

The common mistake. Chapter 16 calls memory a vibing surface: a stale fact, recalled as truth. The worked case is ordinary. A test command from week two is still in the store after you changed it in week four, retrieval finds it on an exact term, the agent runs the wrong command, and reports a pass. Nothing in the answer shows the age of the fact. The fixes: a supersedes field so the correction replaces the original, dates in the injected block, and the authority order from last week, where the file beats the memory of the file. The failure mode is number four, skipped cheap verification. When an attacker plants the stale fact on purpose, OWASP's December 2025 list for agentic applications calls it ASI06, memory and context poisoning.

Nothing in the answer says the fact is five weeks old or that a newer file disagrees.
- Supersedes. A new record names the one it replaces; retrieval drops superseded ids. / Dates in the block. The model and the reader both see the age of what was recalled. / Authority order. The file in the repository beats the memory of the file. In E6 terms a memory is derived (L3); L2 > L1 > L3. / A falsifier on the card: retrieval changes an answer that should not change.
- App. C #4, skipped cheap verification: the agent trusted a recalled command instead of reading the current file. OWASP's agentic top 10 (Dec 2025) names the adversarial version ASI06, memory and context poisoning.

RAG, read for mechanism. Two memories: the weights of a BART generator, and an index of twenty-one million hundred-word Wikipedia chunks that a trained retriever searches by inner product. The design choice is that knowledge lives outside the weights, and the paper's best experiment shows why: swap a 2016 index for a stale one and accuracy on current leaders falls from seventy percent to four. That is a retention result from 2020. The cost is a retriever and an index to maintain. The failure mode is fabrication, because the generator is free to go beyond its passages; provenance only exists if the answer cites what it used.

Cut from slide 16 (full wording):
- A BART-large generator (406M parameters) conditioned on passages that a DPR retriever finds in a dense index of the December 2018 Wikipedia dump: 21M chunks of 100 words, searched by maximum inner product (FAISS). / RAG-Sequence uses the same passages for the whole answer; RAG-Token can draw on a different passage for each token. NeurIPS 2020.
- Choice. Knowledge lives outside the weights, so it can be replaced. The authors swapped indexes: with the 2016 index, 70% of 2016 world-leader questions right; with the 2016 index on 2018 leaders, 4%. / Cost. A retriever to train and an index to keep fresh. / Failure mode. The generator can still answer beyond its passages (App. C #3, fabrication). Retrieval gives provenance only if the answer cites what it used.
- For your system: the index swap is your retention argument. A memory you can replace is a memory you can correct; weights you cannot.

Generative Agents. The mechanism is the memory stream and a retrieval score that adds three things with equal weight: how recent, how important, how relevant. Importance is the model rating each memory from one to ten, which is a model call per observation, and that is the cost. The design choice is reflection: when enough important things have happened, the agent writes higher-level memories that cite the observations behind them. The paper reports its own failures honestly, and they are the ones you will see: a fact that was in memory and not retrieved, and a memory embellished with world knowledge, the neighbor named Adam Smith who suddenly wrote The Wealth of Nations. Fabrication, number three. The strip connects to E9: reflections without pointers become summaries that nobody can check.

Cut from slide 17 (full wording):
- A list of memory objects, each with a description, a creation time, and a last-access time. Retrieval score = recency + importance + relevance, all weights 1. Recency decays by 0.995 per game hour since last access; importance is the model's 1–10 rating.
- When the importance of recent events sums past 150, the agent asks itself questions and stores the answers as higher-level memories that cite their sources. Klaus picks a research partner by reflection, not by who he met most.
- Model calls to rate every observation and to reflect. The paper's own evaluation: agents failed to retrieve (Rajiv had 'not followed the election') and embellished (Yuriko's neighbor Adam Smith 'authored Wealth of Nations'). App. C #3.
- Reflection is memory the model writes about itself. Store it with pointers to its evidence, or it becomes summary laundering inside one agent.

MemGPT to Letta in four steps. The 2023 paper splits the prompt into a read-only system part, a small working block the model edits by function call, and a message queue, with two stores outside. The pager warns at about seventy percent and flushes half the queue into a recursive summary at a hundred. In September 2024 the project became Letta, and the authors asked that MemGPT be used for the pattern and Letta for the framework. The interesting step is this February: Letta Code moved memory into files in a git repository, each change a commit. That is where the reference design started, as you will see at one-thirty. The failure mode is that the model owns its own memory: a wrong fact in the working block is read every turn, and a correction it never saves is gone.

Cut from slide 18 (full wording):
- Main context: system instructions (read-only), working context (a fixed block the model edits only by function call), and a FIFO message queue. External: recall storage (all messages) and archival storage.
- A memory-pressure warning at about 70% of the window; at 100%, about half the queue is evicted into a recursive summary. The model moves facts with function calls; interrupts return control.
- 'MemGPT' becomes the name of the design pattern; Letta is the company and the framework (package letta). Memory blocks with labels such as 'human' and 'persona'.
- Letta Code keeps agent memory as files in a git-backed filesystem. Each change is a commit; subagents merge memory through git; background skills reflect and defragment.
- Three years from custom memory functions to files and commits. Failure mode: the model edits its own working context, so a wrong fact written once is read on every turn, and a correction the model does not save is lost (App. C #5).

Reflexion, in the authors' sentence. Three roles and a tiny episodic memory of one to three lessons in words. The headline is ninety-one percent on HumanEval against eighty for GPT-4 at the time. The mechanism to read is the evaluator: for code, the tests are written by the model. On MBPP one in six of those test runs passed wrong code, and Reflexion did worse there. So the memory is a memory of whatever the evaluator called failure. That is metagaming the gate, number nine, and it is why your Sortie 7 checks answers against the file and not against the model's own grading.

Cut from slide 19 (full wording):

Framing. Read the quote as a list of renamings: manager and contractor in the 1980 contract net, architect and engineer in MetaGPT, main agent and subagent in the harness you use. The division of labor is the same each time. The part that goes missing is a check with authority to stop the work. Two rules. First, a worker returns a typed claim; the controller parses it against a closed set of statuses and rejects anything else, and it never reads a status out of prose. Second, a verdict is evidence only if it cites what was checked and its author could not edit the work. The claim is the chapter's expansion card: nothing merges without a verdict, and FAIL blocks. The falsifiers are pre-registered now, before anyone builds.

Two-stage review, from the reference design. The implementer returns a typed result and the controller parses it. The spec reviewer asks one question: does this change do what the brief says, inside the allowed paths. Only after that passes does the quality reviewer ask whether it is done well. The order matters because a quality reviewer handed the wrong feature will review it carefully and pass it. The controller merges on two cited PASS verdicts, sends CONCERNS to the human, and bounds the retries: after a fixed number of FAIL rounds the task goes BLOCKED to a person rather than looping. For Sortie 8 one reviewer is sound; two stages with separate personas is exceptional.

- Question: is it done well? Tests present and meaningful, errors handled, no dead code. Runs only after spec PASS, so it never polishes the wrong feature.
- Merge only on two PASS verdicts that cite evidence. CONCERNS goes to the human. After N failed rounds the task goes BLOCKED to the human; no silent retry loop.
- Order matters: a quality review of code that does the wrong thing produces a confident PASS on the wrong feature. Your Sortie 8 may use one reviewer; two stages is Exceptional.

First teardown, the classical baseline. The contract net protocol dates to Reid Smith's 1980 paper: call for proposals, propose or refuse, accept one, reject the rest, and the winner reports a result or a failure. FIPA, founded in 1996 and moved to an IEEE standards committee in 2005, standardized the message language, and every message carried a performative. The mechanism to take away: the message type told the receiver what kind of claim it held. The failure mode: the vocabulary never said whether an inform was true, which is fabrication, number three. BDI, from Rao and Georgeff's 1995 paper, made intentions first-class objects with explicit commitment and reconsideration. LLM agents kept the goals and dropped the inspectable belief state. A small aside for the curious: the fipa.org domain no longer hosts the specifications, so cite the IEEE and archived copies. Verify that before you say it in class.

Interoperability through a declared vocabulary. / Cost. Ontologies and heavy tooling. / Failure mode. Nothing said whether an inform was true (#3).

It keeps an intention until it succeeds, becomes impossible, or its reason is gone, and it reconsiders when beliefs change. / What carried forward. Goal decomposition; intent preservation; the halt condition as 'intention achieved or dropped.' The chapter's line: gzkit's intent preservation across context boundaries is BDI's commitment problem with a ledger. / What LLM agents dropped. Explicit belief state that a program can inspect. A chat transcript is not a belief base.

Second teardown, the 2023 role systems. CAMEL set two agents talking with inception prompts, and the paper is honest about what went wrong: role flipping, repeated instructions, flake replies, infinite loops. Its halt is the assistant saying a special token, which is completion by assertion, fabrication and metagaming in one line. MetaGPT is the correction: roles modeled on a software company, connected by structured documents through a publish-subscribe pool, with executable feedback for the engineer. It reported high HumanEval and MBPP numbers for its time. The failure mode is that every role reads the same upstream documents, so a wrong requirement flows through intact. The third card is the lesson for your build: documents with a shape beat chat, and a closed status set plus a blocking verdict is one more step.

Third teardown: roles became configuration. AutoGen's classic design made coordination a conversation: an assistant writes code, a user proxy runs it and can pull in a human, and a group chat manager picks who speaks next. Its best feature was that code actually ran, so there was an observation in the loop. Its halt was a TERMINATE string. As of this year the AutoGen repository is in maintenance mode and points new users to Microsoft Agent Framework, which reached 1.0 on April 3, 2026, with sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, and Magentic-One orchestrations plus checkpointing and human approvals. CrewAI made coordination an org chart: the hierarchical manager plans, delegates, and reviews. Its guardrail is the closest thing in the survey to your contract: a function returns a boolean and a value, with retries. The failure to watch: a retry loop against a checker can be metagamed.

Fourth teardown, the LangGraph supervisor. The mechanism is a hub node that routes to workers and gets control back, with a checkpointer under everything. The old library made the key trade-off a single parameter: give the supervisor every worker message, or only the last one. Full history costs window; last message costs visibility, and a supervisor that sees only a worker's summary treats it as the result, which is summary laundering. In 2026 LangChain's own advice is to build the supervisor with tool calling so you control exactly what each subagent receives and returns, and its multi-agent page names five patterns. For your build: whatever passes back through your controller should be the typed result plus a pointer to the evidence, not the worker's prose.

- Choice: the controller is code you can read, and the supervisor is one node in it, not the whole program. / Cost: every routing decision is a model call at the hub; full_history fills the supervisor's window, last_message hides the worker's trace. - Failure: with last_message the supervisor sees only the worker's summary and treats it as the result (#3, summary laundering). / 2026: LangChain recommends the supervisor built directly with tool calling, for control over what each subagent receives and returns. The reference design. ADR-0.18.0 defines a five-stage pipeline: load context, implement with two-stage review per task, verify, present evidence, and sync. The controller never implements; it dispatches, parses, and decides. Stage three is the controller running the checks itself, which is why a worker's claim that tests pass is not verification. Stage four presents paths and commands rather than conclusions, and in E9 you will see the adversarial step inserted there. Stage five writes the ledger events and the dispatch records, and the human attests. The files to read are the subagent-pipeline concept document, roles.py, pipeline_dispatch.py, and the persona directory. Verify the ADR number, the stage names, and the paths against the repository before class.

The mechanism that makes the pipeline auditable. Both result types are parsed fail-closed. Every dispatch of every role writes a record, and the rule is that credit is never inferred: no record for a role means the role did not run, whatever any summary says. The right panel is the honesty flag. A run where one agent did everything is allowed, but it must be declared with a reason, and the course takes the same line: a declared single-driver run is graded as what it is, and an undeclared one presented as reviewed fails. If your reviewer cannot run because the model is unavailable or you hit your usage limit, that is an abort, and the log says so. Verify which command takes the flag before class.

Weak: a reviewer that is the implementer in the same session, a verdict read by substring, a parser that defaults to DONE, a reviewer with write access, a persona that claims expertise, and a loop with no saved state and no human. Sound: a separate read-only reviewer declared in configuration, two schemas with closed status sets, malformed input rejected and logged, FAIL that blocks and a bound on rounds, findings with locations, a graph with a checkpoint and an interrupt, and a dispatch record per role. Exceptional: two-stage review, a reviewer on a different model, the anti-trait ablation measured, an honest squawk for a defect the reviewer missed, and a Chase who re-runs the evidence commands rather than reading them.

Framing. Last week's pair gave you a contract, and a contract tells you the shape of a claim, not whether it is true. Two rules. First, a claim needs a receipt that the harness wrote: command, exit code, commit, output hash. Second, the check comes from something with different blind spots, and the cheapest different thing is a different model family. The claim is the chapter 18 corner card. Notice the second falsifier: if you plant a falsehood and your adversary lets it through, the sortie fails, which means you will know before you fly whether your adversary is a real one.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- A worker that says “all tests pass” has produced a sentence. The harness that ran the tests and wrote down the exit code has produced evidence.
- Rule one. A claim moves toward the flight log only with a receipt: the command, the exit code, the commit, and a hash of the output, written by the harness and never by a model. / Rule two. The check comes from something that does not share the worker's blind spots: a second model family first, an independent subagent second, a human third. A reviewer that shares the worker's model shares its mistakes.
- A subagent's claim never becomes evidence without a receipt, and a second-family adversary refutes a false claim that you planted. Any one of these falsifies it: a claim in the flight log with no receipt; the adversary returning NOT-REFUTED on the planted falsehood; a lock held by two workers, or a lock change with no ledger event.

The taxonomy, by the paper's three categories. The shares are the paper's own prevalence figures summed by category; they add to about one hundred percent across the three. Design failures are the largest group, and the top single mode is step repetition, which is a halt problem you met in week one. Misalignment is the traffic between agents; the top mode there is a reasoning-action mismatch, where the agent says one thing and does another. Verification is the last line: incorrect verification alone is nine percent of failures, which is a reviewer that checked and got it wrong. The strip adds the two names from the reference design. Summary laundering is FC2 and FC3 at once: the information passes, and nobody checks it.

This table is the vocabulary for the week. A claim is a sentence a model wrote; it goes in the ledger marked unverified and never in the flight log. A receipt is what the harness observed when it ran the command itself, and it is the only row here that is evidence about the code. The adversary's verdict is also a claim, from a different author; the Chase checks that its citation points at a real field in the receipt. The attestation is the human's and is never inferred. The strip is the sentence most students get wrong in their flight logs: not refuted is not verified.

Three tiers. Tier one is a different family because the failure you are guarding against is a shared blind spot, and the self-preference result gives you the measured reason: evaluators score their own generations higher. Tier two is a fresh subagent of the same family, which removes the shared transcript but not the shared training. Tier three is a person. On the right, the practical news: with OpenCode Go, a second family costs almost nothing, and I checked the prices on the Go page this week; verify them again before you fly. Big Pickle's family is undisclosed, so you cannot prove it differs from your adversary; two adversaries from two named families solve that for pennies. If you only have one family, the reference design's rule applies: run in degraded mode and say so on the card.

- Tier 1 · cross-vendor. A different model family. It does not share the worker's training data, tokenizer, or house style, so it is least likely to find the worker's mistake plausible. Same family, fresh context, no access to the worker's transcript. Cheaper to arrange; shares the family's blind spots. / Tier 3 · human. The Chase, or you. Slowest; the only tier that can attest.
- Tier 1 is cheap this term. Write “worker family: undisclosed,” and run two adversaries from two Go families to close the gap. / No Go subscription: use a free Zen model from a named family (Nemotron, MiMo). - The adversary gets the claim and the receipt. It never gets the worker's summary, its reasoning, or the answer you planted.

Three pieces you can copy. The agent file is OpenCode's markdown agent format: a subagent with its own model and every write-class permission denied, so the adversary can read what you attach and nothing else. The prompt asks for one JSON object and defines NOT-REFUTED in the prompt itself, because a model left to its own words will write verified. The receipt is written by your harness when it runs the test command; the model never touches it. The ledger event records the model id and the family, which is what the Chase checks. The last line is the non-interactive form: opencode run with an agent and attached files, which is how you will call it from a script in the Sprint.

Locks in four steps. The atomic create is the whole trick: O_EXCL makes the operating system the referee, so you do not need a lock server for one laptop. The second worker is denied and says who holds the lock; it does not wait forever and it does not overwrite. Release needs the token, so a confused worker cannot free someone else's lock. The TTL handles the worker that crashed while holding it, and the expiry is recorded before the reclaim so the order is visible in the ledger. The reference design has a lock verb for exactly this, and the chapter calls the ledger the lock's witness. The strip is the card's falsifier, stated carefully.

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- Create locks/<resource>.lock with os.open(path, O_CREAT | O_EXCL). The operating system lets exactly one caller create it. Write {holder, token, acquired_at, ttl_s}. / Ledger: lock_acquired.
- A second worker's create fails with FileExistsError. It does not wait silently and does not overwrite. It returns BLOCKED with the holder's name. / Ledger: lock_denied.
- Only the caller holding the token may delete the lock. A release with the wrong token is refused. / Ledger: lock_released.
- If now > acquired_at + ttl_s, the holder is presumed dead. The next worker records the expiry before it takes the lock. / Ledger: lock_expired, then lock_acquired.
- The falsifier is not “two workers collided.” It is a lock that changed hands with no ledger event, because then nobody can tell whether the collision happened.

Routing. The idea is old and the numbers are published: route easy work to a cheap model and hard work to an expensive one. RouteLLM, from the same Berkeley group as the MAST paper, reported more than eighty-five percent lower cost on MT Bench while keeping ninety-five percent of GPT-4's quality; FrugalGPT's cascades reported up to ninety-eight percent lower cost. Your version is a table in config, one row per task class, and a budget line on the card. The prices are the Go page's as of this week. Two things to notice: Kimi K3 costs twenty times glm-5.3-flash on output and allows about a hundred and ten requests per five hours, so it belongs on the rows where a mistake propagates; and the adversary row needs a different family, not a bigger model. The reference design keeps a dispatch model map for the same purpose.

The result contract says what evidence each status needs; fail closed, so a DONE with no receipt is treated as needing context. The evidence obligation says who writes the receipt, and if it is the worker, it is not a receipt. The strip is the one thing that does not cross: the human's authority. When a peer needs it, the protocol has states for asking, and your host answers.

A production system, with numbers. Fifteen times the tokens of a chat, and token usage alone explains eighty percent of the variance on their browsing benchmark, which tells you the gain is bought with spend. The failures are MAST failures: duplicated work and over-spawning are FC1 and FC2, and the fix was specification, which matches the paper's intervention. CIDM6333_MiniLecture_Attention2017.pptx: Twenty minutes on one paper. We read "Attention Is All You Need" the way we read every system in this course: as a design document. What constraint did the authors face, what did they trade, and what evidence did they offer? The model behind OpenCode and Big Pickle is a descendant of this design. The three explainer figures on the course site carry everything I show tonight, so you can step through them later.

Five moves. The constraint first, because a design makes sense only against the problem it answers. Then the mechanism, then the evidence, which is the part most summaries skip. Then what chat models kept from the 2017 design, and finally why any of it matters to someone building a harness.

Read the highlighted row against the recurrent row. Self-attention gives up a constant amount of sequential work and a constant path length between any two words, which is why it trains fast on GPUs and why distant words can affect each other. The price is n squared times d per layer. The paper argues that price is fine when n is smaller than d, which was true of 2017 sentences. Keep that sentence in mind: it stopped being true when context windows reached a million tokens, and that is the cost Evolution 6 asks you to budget.

Cut from slide 3 (full wording):
- What the authors faced / A recurrent network reads token 1, then token 2, then token 3. Each step waits for the one before it, so training cannot spread a sentence across a GPU. / The paper's trade: let every position look at every other position at once. The sequential chain drops from O(n) to O(1); the compute per layer grows with n².

This is the paper's Figure 1 redrawn. The left stack reads the source sentence; the right stack writes the target. Each stack repeats one layer six times. Notice there is no arrow from the top back to the bottom in the paper, yet section 3 says the model is auto-regressive: it consumes what it generated. That missing arrow is the inner loop from Figure 01, Two Loops. Figure 01b on the course site steps through every box with the paper's own words.

Cut from slide 4 (full wording):
- Figure 1, redrawn: two stacks and a loop the paper describes

One line of math. Queries, keys, and values are three projections of the same input. The dot product of a query with every key gives a score; softmax turns scores into weights; the weights mix the values. The paper makes two choices worth naming. It divides by the square root of d_k because large dot products saturate softmax. And in the decoder it masks the future by setting those scores to minus infinity. The grid on the right uses random vectors, so it shows the arithmetic, not meaning. In Figure 01b, switch scaling off and raise d_k: the rows collapse onto one key, which is the saturation the paper describes.

Two more pieces. Multi-head attention runs eight smaller attentions side by side, each 64 wide, so the total work equals one 512-wide head; the heads can specialize. Table 3 tested this: one head loses 0.9 BLEU, and too many heads also hurt. Second, attention by itself has no idea of word order. The paper adds a fixed pattern of waves to each token vector, fast waves in the low dimensions and slow waves in the high ones. Learned positions worked about as well. Many newer models encode position differently, but the problem is the same one.

Cut from slide 6 (full wording):
- Eight heads at once, and word order written in waves

Table 2 is the headline. The big Transformer scores 28.4 BLEU on English to German, more than two points above everything before it, ensembles included. The base model already beats them. Now look at how the paper reports cost: it does not claim a measured number. It multiplies training time by the number of GPUs by each GPU's rated throughput, and it prints the rated throughputs in a footnote. You can recompute it: 12 hours times 3600 times 8 GPUs times 9.5 teraflops is about 3.3 times ten to the eighteenth. A number with its method beside it is a receipt. And notice the French result: the table says 41.8 and the text says 41.0. Even a famous paper has a mismatch; the table is the table of record. Figure 01c on the course site plots this against cost on a log scale.

Cut from slide 7 (full wording):
- Evidence 1: better translations at a fraction of the training cost

Table 3 is my favorite part of the paper because it is an evaluation design. Each row changes one thing against the same base model, and every score comes from a development set, not the test set used in Table 2. Read the bars: two layers instead of six costs 2.1 BLEU; turning off dropout costs 1.2; one head costs 0.9; a bigger model gains a little. Learned positions change almost nothing. That is the shape of the delta gate you build in Evolution 10: fixed baseline, one change, held-out set, and a threshold you commit to before you look. Ask yourself which of these rows you would believe from a single run.

Cut from slide 8 (full wording):
- Evidence 2: change one thing, measure against a fixed base

The architecture does not train itself. Equation 3 raises the learning rate in a straight line for the first 4,000 steps and then lets it fall with the inverse square root of the step. The grey line shows a longer warmup: a lower peak, reached later. The rest of the recipe matters as much: Adam with an unusual beta two of 0.98, dropout everywhere, and label smoothing, which the paper admits makes perplexity worse while BLEU improves. When you compare models in Evolution 10, you compare recipes too.

Cut from slide 9 (full wording):
- The rest of the recipe / Adam with β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.98, ε = 10⁻⁹. / Dropout 0.1 on every sub-layer output and on the embeddings. / Label smoothing 0.1: it "hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score." / Base: 100,000 steps. Big: 300,000 steps.

Here is the same figure with the encoder faded out. GPT in 2018 kept only the right-hand column: embeddings, masked self-attention, feed-forward, add and norm, and the softmax head. The prompt and the reply become one sequence. Two other changes matter to you. Chat models sample their next token instead of running beam search, so output varies from run to run; that is why one run is an anecdote in Evolution 10. And most later models move the normalization step before each sub-layer, which trains more stably at depth.

Five lines from the paper to this course. The n squared term is your context budget. The softmax at the top of Figure 1 is where the paper stops and your harness starts: reading the reply, gating the tool call, feeding the result back, deciding when to halt. Sampling is why you run evals more than once. Table 3 is the model for your delta gate. And the cost estimate is a model for every number you put in a flight log: show the method so your Chase can recompute it.

- One run is an anecdote. Run the golden set several times and gate on the delta.

One sentence to carry out: a design document names its constraint, its trade, and its evidence. Use that test on every system in your Design Analysis this week. Welcome to CIDM 6333, Agentic Systems Design and Development. I am Dr. Jeffry Babb. This deck is the orientation: what the course is, how each Thursday runs, what you will build, what you will analyze, how it is scored, and the choices you have to make this week about models, harnesses, frameworks, and kits. The syllabus governs dates and policy. Everything about the weekly mechanics lives here and in WTClass, not in the syllabus. Four words on the slide describe the semester: survey the systems, build your own, govern the build, and defend it in person.

Cut from slide 1 (full wording):
- Orientation · Fall 2026 · Thursdays 4:00–6:30 · CC209

Two questions, one course. The first is a survey question: why are these systems designed the way they are? Not what is fashionable this month, but what problem each design answered and what it cost. The second is a build question: can you make one, and can you answer for it? The Tree Hollow essay is your first reading because it names the stake. A model can produce an answer it cannot answer for. In this course, you are the one who answers, and the whole structure of the semester, the flight cards, the consultations, the attestations, exists to make that true rather than aspirational.

- Why are agentic systems designed the way they are — and can you build one you can answer for?
- Every week we take two or three real systems apart against one component model, in historical order, and ask why each part is built the way it is. You write one Design Analysis per week. By December you have traced the field from symbolic agents to today’s harnesses and protocols.
- You choose one agentic system on day one and add a layer to it every week: loop, patterns, tools, MCP, context, memory, multi-agent, evaluation, deployment. Every layer is flown against a flight card and defended face to face.
- “A system can produce an answer without being able to answer for it.” — Sprint and Drift, Tree Hollow (this week’s essay). The course is about being the one who answers.

This is the first of two maps you will use all semester. Seven layers. Agentic AI on top: memory, planning, tool use, autonomous execution. Underneath it, generative AI, deep learning, neural networks, machine learning, classical AI, and at the bottom, the data foundation, the one everybody forgets: ownership, definitions, data quality, lineage. Every agentic system you analyze stands on all of these. When you write a Design Analysis, start at the bottom: what model, what weights, what data does this thing stand on, local or hosted? You will feel the foundation most in week seven, when you build memory on embeddings, and in week eleven, when you ask what your evaluation data actually is.

The second map. Five stages, left to right. AI and ML turns data into decisions. Deep learning stacks networks for complex tasks. Generative AI creates content. Before the LLM there was a perfectly good definition of an agent: something that perceives its environment and acts on it, specified by PEAS. The LLM agent loop is that definition with a model as the reasoner: perceive, reason, act, repeat until a halt condition. Most of what went wrong in 2023 was the halt condition. The nine components on the right are how you will take every system apart this semester: what it stands on, what it sees, how it plans, how it uses tools, what it remembers, how it coordinates, what evaluates it, where the human is, and how it runs. A Design Analysis is nine short answers and one paragraph on why.

Cut from slide 5 (full wording):
- An agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts through actuators. Specify it by PEAS: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors. This definition predates LLMs and still holds.
- Perceive (prompt, tool results) → Reason (model call) → Act (tool call or answer) → repeat until a halt condition. ReAct (2022) is the canonical form. The halt condition is the part 2023 forgot.

Here is why the course is built the way it is. The degradation pattern: week one you read every line; week four you are approving pull requests you never read. Nobody decides to lose control; it slips away one looks-good at a time. The Zero Doctrine is the answer and it comes from gzkit: the human is index zero, first in priority, final in authority, and that role cannot be automated away. The covenant has two sides. Gates constrain the agents. Humans must engage. If you only have gates, you get theater: every check passes and nobody verified anything. So every build in this course is governed, every week you defend it without the tool, every claim is falsifiable before it is flown, and your AI log is something we talk about, not something you file.

A flight card is a one-page form you fill in before you touch the terminal. It comes from gzkit’s flight-test program, which borrowed it from aircraft flight test: nobody just flies it and sees. Envelope position says how far from the known-good center this sortie goes. The design claim is one sentence that a single observation could disprove. Test points are the path you will fly and the observable you expect at each step. Instrumentation is what must appear in the black box. The falsifiers are written before the run; if any one appears, the sortie failed. A Chase reads the evidence cold and writes the verdict. Then you debrief and route every squawk somewhere. Five rules bind all of this, and the last one matters most: the Chase never sees your narrative, only your evidence.

- Five binding rules: pre-register the falsifier · the black box (ledger, receipts, traces) is truth, never prose or a status screen · build up the envelope center → expansion → corner · fly the governed path (no hand-written markers, no --no-verify) · independent observation by a Chase who did not fly it.

Here is the card for week three, written the way I want yours written. The claim is one sentence and it is falsifiable: no write-tool executes without a prior confirmation event. Four test points, in order, each with the observable that must appear in the black box. Test point four is the interesting one: the file the agent reads contains a prompt injection asking for a write, and the gate must still fire. The falsifiers are written before you run anything, and the last one is the anti-vibing tripwire: passing only by disabling the gate is a fail. The abort criterion keeps a broken Ollama install from being scored as a design failure. The Chase gets the ledger slice and the receipts, not your story.

The first is the reference design’s missing piece: gzkit deliberately does not speak MCP, so an MCP server over the gz verbs and the ledger is both useful and a good teardown question. Whatever you choose, ask one question: can I add every one of the twelve layers to this? If memory or a second agent or serving would be artificial, pick something else.

Your harness is where the model works inside your repository, and it is also one of the systems we take apart, because each one encodes a theory of control. By week two you commit to an orchestration layer in ADR-1, with alternatives and consequences, and you defend it in Drift. The table is the argument space. The Claude Agent SDK gives you the Claude Code harness as a library, with hooks and MCP built in, at the price of one vendor. LangGraph makes the agent a state graph you own edge by edge.
